estimates.basis: The older John Glasgow who held the Saltmarket Rankin–Young tenement in 1527 is assessed as the probable father of William Glasgow-1098. William occupies the matching parcel by 20 February 1528/29; the later St Andrew prebend rental retains its four-shilling burden, west-side street position and Rankin boundary. The 1534 family settlement and 1564 service as heir then directly identify the younger John Glasgow-1093 as William’s son. Read together, these describe a sustained family title rather than merely two men sharing a surname. Lineal succession from the earlier John to William is the preferred reconstruction, while the last William-to-John step is independently documented. The grade is now probable, below documented or strongly supported. This brings the formal local father assessment into line with the stronger property argument already developed in the research. The missing 1527–1529 conveyance has not been found. No inspected instrument calls William the earlier John’s son, and no recorded ages distinguish father from brother. A brother, collateral heir or purchase from a namesake remains possible. Indeed, the neighbouring Henryson parcel in the 1528/29 instrument passes between brothers; title succession alone cannot specify kinship. The combined parcel descriptions are correlated, and the later rental is not an independent record of the original transfer. Glasgow-1095 remains a provisional representation of the Saltmarket owner: its identification with the Stirling witness or the 1506 alias-Smith purchaser is not proved. The probable grade applies to the property-defined Saltmarket father hypothesis, not to every imported biographical claim. No mother is inferred: Eufame Craig may have been the earlier John’s widow, but this does not establish her as William’s mother. No Stirling parent, birth estimate, death location or identity merge is upgraded. The live WikiTree father flag remains uncertain; probable is a local research grade.

Prefer the existing James Glasgow-991 and Christina Bie-55 family account for the Fisherrow James and Christina Bye. The printed 1624–1625 index explicitly groups James, tailor in Fisherrow and burgess of Musselburgh, his son Alexander and wife Christina Bye; it separately names Alexander’s wife Janet Clerk. Those are the same named family roles already represented by these profiles. The local James account also includes the Inveresk father sequence of 1609–1618, which can continue into the Fisherrow household. The ordinary Bye/Bie spelling and the full family fit make the identification probable, rather than a match resting only on James’s forename. This is an assessment of the preferred existing family account, not independent confirmation from its copied tree fields. The Mid Calder and Inveresk baptism sequences may still represent one mobile father or two contemporaries; no occupation or property recital joins them. The profile’s birth and death places remain inherited claims. The signed-in FamilySearch record VQ4V-K87 was inspected on 17 October 2026: it names William, father James and the 10 July 1614 Inveresk event, but no mother. It therefore supplies no independent evidence for Christina Bie’s maternity, consistent with the FMP and supplied ScotlandsPeople entries. The earlier citation-based claim that this record named her is withdrawn; the underlying parish image remains uninspected. Christina’s 1589 New Aberdour birth is tree-derived. Naming her as James’s wife in 1624 does not establish her as Alexander’s or William’s mother. The Andrew-3163 and Murieston-George ancestry alternatives retain their grades.

Select Stephen Glasgow-1029 as the uncertain working father of James Glasgow-3910. A Stephen born around the mid-sixteenth century could have fathered James in the 1570s–1590s and John in a similar generation. Select the Quothquan weaver James Glasgow-3910 as the uncertain working father of Helen Glasgow-3909, the married Thankerton woman whose testament was indexed in January 1627. The shared uncommon surname, neighbouring Quothquan/Thankerton locality and an adult weaver recorded at the 1612 hearing followed by a married woman dead by 1627 give a coherent father/daughter generation. Helen’s circa-1605 birth is an inherited estimate, not her stated age; it is compatible with a James born before the mid-1590s but is not independent proof of that generation. This is a low-confidence local family selection. No inspected record calls Helen James’s daughter.

Select John Glasgow-1030 as the very low-confidence working father of Matthew Glasgow-3538 of Pyperheugh, Stevenston. John and Jonet Mathie married in Glasgow on 25 January 1618 and have recorded children in the following decade. A son of that household, born in the 1620s, could be an adult spouse in the 1665 testament index that names Matthew. This is a compatible generation, not a new birth estimate. The existing Mathie–Glasgow network supplies a positive social route between Glasgow and Stevenston: David Mathy and Robert Glasgow were co-witnesses in 1554, while Matthew Glasgow and John Mathie were together at Ardeer Nether in 1559–60. The later marriage joins those surname networks. The recurrence of Matthew in the same parish makes this existing household a useful selected descent hypothesis; it does not identify a father in a record.

Select William Glasgow-3075, the Leith mealmaker, as the low-confidence working father of Margaret Glasgow-3186, indexed marrying George Lyell at South Leith on 28 November 1633. William’s household is documented at Leith, with a proposed 10 July 1610 local marriage and a son Archibald baptised in 1618, securely linked to the adult mealmaker by the 1639 apprenticeship and 1647 service of heir. A daughter marrying in 1633 fits that established household generation. Shared surname, the same parish and a coherent marriage/child generation favour this named household over a newly invented father. No source calls Margaret his daughter. Her circa-1610 birth remains an inherited estimate and supplies no independent evidence of William’s paternity.

Select Robert Glaskow of Larne, Glasgow-3970, as the very low-confidence working father of Elizabeth Glasgow-3961, the Eliz Glascho at Glenarm Town in 1669. Robert is an older recorded adult at Larne in 1653, and the existing uncertain paternal family already includes John Glasgow-3913 and James Glasgow-1081, the adjacent Jo/James Glascho householders at Kilwaughter in the same 1669 roll. Elizabeth shares their unusual recorded Glascho form and the east-Antrim setting. Her assumed adult-householder generation in 1669 can be a daughter generation of the earlier Larne man. This extends an existing local family explanation rather than inventing an unnamed father; no record calls Elizabeth his daughter or John’s sister.

Select John Glasgow-3375, the father associated with Barbara Alason/Allason at Kilwinning in 1679 and 1689, as the uncertain working father of James Glasgow-4170, father with Mary Auld at Stevenston in 1717–1718. This is a low/very low-confidence regional household placement. The recorded couple supplies a compatible parent generation, and their son John Glasgow-1434, indexed at Kilwinning in 1679, is already a possible identity for the John who had children with Margaret Cowan at Stevenston in 1701 and 1706. That existing route gives a specific neighbouring-parish family comparison for James’s later Stevenston household. The preferred provisional model places James alongside that John as a possible paternal brother. It does not identify a baptism for James or claim that the 1717–1718 entries name his parents.

Select Johne Glasgow-3093, indexed at Mid Calder in 1648 as son of Jamis Glasgow, as the very low-confidence working father of Robert Glasgow-4168, father at Libberton in 1718–1726. The preferred local route runs through Johne’s existing uncertain James-3332 father identity and that James’s possible identification with the Lindsaylands weaver indexed in 1680. Lindsaylands and Quothquan/Libberton supply the adjacent Lanarkshire family setting; Mid Calder is a separate parish and no migration is proved. A Johne born around 1648 could father Robert in the 1680s–1690s, allowing ordinary adult fatherhood at the 1718 baptism. This generation is preferred over assigning Robert directly to the older weaver, who was dead by 1680 if that identity is correct. It is a specific family hypothesis using recorded men, not a father clause in Robert’s records.

Select John Glasgow-1105 and Agnes Eastone-3 as the uncertain working parents of Thomas Glasgow-1226, the father with Catherine Clarkson/Classon at Uphall from 1717 and Livingston by 1730. This selects possible identity with their named Linlithgow child Thomas Glasgow-1242 of 1675, while retaining both profile accounts. That child would be about 42 at the 1717 Margaret entry and about 60 at the 1735 Hellen entry: later fatherhood, but chronologically possible. The existing Glasgow-1242 account also represents a Thomas/Jean Duncan household at Uphall in 1704. Recurring Thomas name, the same Uphall parish and a plausible succession of households provide a more specific route than the removed Kilbirnie-minister parents. The 1675 parent clause belongs directly to the child account; transferring it to the Clarkson adult depends wholly on the uncertain identity.

Select Thomas Glasgow-1242 as the uncertain working father of Philip Glasco-146. The preferred model uses Glasco-146 as the elder Dublin watchmaker account, retaining the 1711 Scottish child Glasgow-1241 as a separate possible account of the same man. That child’s Uphall index names father Thomas; his existing research already retains the elder watchmaker as a compatible adult identity. The Glasco-146 account has the Christ Church Lane watchmaking association in 1752, an estimated birth about 1715 and a younger Philip in its tree family, which suit that provisional elder role. The four-year difference from the 1711 baptism is between a record and an unsupported estimate, not a concrete identity conflict. This materialises the existing Scottish candidate at low confidence; it does not prove migration or two distinct elder Philips.

Select Hugh Glasgow-3109, father with Jean Service at Irvine in 1696, as the very low-confidence working father of James Glasgow-4158, father with Margaret/Marion Rae at Irvine in 1721–1723. This extends an actual local household across a compatible generation. A James born in the later 1690s could be a son of the 1696 household and an adult father by 1721; this is a compatibility example, not a new birth estimate. Hugh’s proposed identity with the 1676 Kilwinning child would make him a young father in the 1690s, which fits that example. The shared uncommon surname, same parish and two successive family generations favour this existing named parent model; no register entry names James’s father.

Select William Glasgow-1026 as the uncertain working father of John Glasgow-3481, the combined Calder father account recorded in 1730 and with Christian Meek in 1751–1755. This adopts possible identity with John Glasgow-1544, the child indexed at Kirknewton in 1702 with father William. The same name and parish and a normal adult generation favour this concrete child account over an unidentified origin: if baptised near birth in 1702, he would be about 28 in 1730 and 53 at the 1755 child. Those ages are conditional examples, not ages stated in the registers. The old circa 1710 birth was inferred from assumed age at the 1730 fatherhood and cannot exclude the 1702 child. The child’s existing father identity as William-1026 is itself qualified; no record explicitly identifies the later Meek husband as his son.

Select John Glasgow-1057 and Agnes Spark-330 as the uncertain working parents of George Glasgow-4165, father with Margt at Irvine in 1741–1745. The preferred model uses possible identity with their son George Glasgow-1058, baptised at Kilwinning on 20 November 1687 and already associated with the George/Margaret Martain couple indexed marrying there on 11 June 1728. That couple’s son George-3312 is indexed at Kilwinning in 1729. The nearby Irvine household later repeats George and Margt, with no maternal surname or father’s age stated. This offers a specific existing couple and a compatible continuation across neighbouring parishes. On an infant-baptism assumption, the elder George would be about 54–58 at the Irvine children; late fatherhood remains possible. Margaret’s circa 1704 estimate would fit an adult mother in 1741–1745, but it is only a marriage-derived estimate. Neither calculation proves the identities or a move.

Glasgow-2462 is the proposed, very uncertain working father of the traditional Ulster ancestor Glasgow-591 and the Cavers Covenanter Glasgow-4138. This carries the existing possible identity with the Polwarth child Glasgow-1605 into a concrete local family model. The Polwarth index names the child’s father as William Glasgow, and Glasgow-2462 is already attached to that child with uncertainty. The three younger profile accounts are retained as possible stages of one life, not three proved brothers. Neither new father attachment is independent support for the other: both depend on the same child/adult identity and on the unproved identification of the named Polwarth father with the Inveresk man. The Polwarth child was baptised on 4 April 1658. If baptised near birth, he would have been about 21 at the examination of the Cavers servant in June 1679, 26 at the Ormistoun servant list in 1684 and 31 in 1689. Those are compatible ages for the recorded adult and the later military tradition. The Ulster profile’s circa 1656 birth is explicitly a rough grandson-based estimate, not an age stated by a record; its guessed Glasgow-city origin cannot exclude a Borders childhood. The exact forename and surname, compatible sequence and existing Borders candidate make this a usable provisional life model. Polwarth and Cavers are distinct parishes in different counties, and the chronology supplies compatibility rather than an identifying age match. The Cavers setting is recorded residence/association, not a proved birthplace. The Cavers man is the leading existing Scottish comparison for Glasgow-591 because the records establish a Covenanter and wreck survivor before the reported 1689 episode, while a probable member of his actual parish survivor group, James Young, appears among survivors said to have reached Ulster. Waddell’s 1886 account says all fifty survivors reached northern Ireland; his revised 1902 account says only some and omits both Glasgows from its named list. The omission does not exclude William, but the revision and late publication weaken the blanket migration claim. The 1684 Ormistoun record also prevents assuming uninterrupted Ulster residence from 1679. The later family history’s 1689 service and settlement remain tradition, not verified military service. No particular crossing, return journey, unit or Irish residence is invented. Its Cameron-to-Glasgow surname-origin story cannot explain a man already called Glasgow in 1679.

Glasgow-1509, the older Larne ropemaker, is selected as the uncertain working father of Adam of Inishrush (Glasgow-3902). This adopts the named-family comparison already tested in September. Adam’s gravestone age implies birth about 1758; James’s reported 1737 birth would give an ordinary age-21 generation. The original 1773 affidavit independently places the Larne James’s birth before October 1743, although it does not prove the reported 1737 year. Adam’s proved son James (Glasgow-3903) supplies limited positive naming support. James is a documented adult with a trade and property trail, making him a more useful provisional father than the recordless Glasgow-3905 placeholder. No record names Adam as his child, and the naming argument is weak rather than corroboration of a parent clause. A 1760 lease identifies James as a Belfast ropemaker taking a ropewalk at Gardenmore, Larne; the 1768 assignment identifies the same property. This is a real occupational and locality sequence, distinct from the contemporary Larne tanner. Adam is documented much later at Inishrush, and the monument does not state his birthplace. The estimated Inishrush birth cannot exclude a family from elsewhere, but no Belfast birth or Larne-to-Inishrush migration is newly assigned. The 1773 Larne gentleman’s age excludes the younger Glasgow-3991 account; the identity assessment and separation of the two trades retain their previous grades. The reported James/Shutter-46 marriage in 1762 is later than Adam’s birth. It cannot establish Shutter-46 as Adam’s mother. An earlier union, premarital birth or inaccurate reported date would be needed if this father model is right; no such event or person is invented. Shutter-46 is not selected as older Alexander’s mother either: the marriage report and the son identity are independently unproved.

The same James is selected, with very low confidence, as father of the reconstructed older Alexander (Glasgow-3904). This adopts the existing possible-brother route for Adam and Alexander. On the reported 1737 and estimated 1770 years, James would be about 33 at Alexander’s birth. Making Adam, born about 1758, Alexander’s father instead produces a twelve-year interval. Alexander’s circa 1770 birth is only an estimate, so that calculation does not exclude an Adam father: Alexander could have been born later. However, fatherhood of Daniel by about 1795/96 places Alexander in a generation born by roughly 1775–1778, leaving two short successive generations in the Adam-to-Alexander model. Adam’s wife Unknown-760890, born about 1766/67 from her monument age, cannot be Alexander’s mother on that chronology. The sibling route is therefore preferred provisionally without inventing an earlier wife. Chronological economy does not prove brotherhood or a shared father; neither selected edge is independent support for the other. John Glasgow-3375 is the selected uncertain working father of the West Kilbride parent John Glasgow-3161, through possible identity with his son Jon Glasgow-1434, indexed at Kilwinning on 6 July 1679. The West Kilbride account already names Glasgow-1434 as an identity comparison. A child born near the 1679 baptism could have been about twenty at the January 1700 Patrick event, followed by the John/Margaret Cowan children at nearby Stevenston in 1701 and 1706 if that further adult identity is right. This supplies a specific neighbouring-parish household and ordinary generation, preferred provisionally to leaving the 1700 father without a named family. It does not prove that the Kilwinning child, Stevenston father and West Kilbride father were one person.

The West Kilbride John Glasgow-3161 is the selected uncertain working father of Rev. Patrick Glasgow-635, through possible identity with the indexed child Patrick Glasgow-3160 of 1700. The minister’s church-history account calls him Patrick, and the previously reviewed biography of his son calls the father a native of Scotland. If the 1700 child became the minister, he would have been about thirty-five when son James was born in 1735, thirty-six when ordained at Manokin in 1736, and fifty-three at his death in 1753. That is a coherent adult career and family sequence. The recorded Scottish childhood and compatible dates make this a useful low-confidence choice; no ministerial, marriage or migration record identifies that child as the Maryland man. The inherited 1680 minister birth is an unsupported estimate and would contradict this childhood route if literal.

James Glasgow-3332 is the selected uncertain working father of Robert Glasgow-3407, who married Katherine Wilson at Carnwath in 1713 and is associated with son John Glasgow-2870 at Libberton in 1722. This is conditional on James representing the weaver at Back of Lindsaylands whose testament was indexed in 1680. The adjacent Biggar, Libberton and Carnwath family setting supplies a specific local comparison. A James born around the inherited 1630/1634 estimates could father Robert in the 1660s or 1670s; a Robert born in the 1670s could marry in 1713 and father John in 1722 at ordinary adult ages. This provisional older-generation route is preferred to making the two overlapping Libberton Roberts sons of the same Johne. No record names Robert as the weaver’s child. Robert’s current circa-1690 birth estimate would be too late for a father dead by 1680; an earlier birth is required if this hypothesis is right. That estimate is unsupported, but the required revision remains a limitation, not evidence for the proposed father.

John Glasgow-3375 is the selected very uncertain working father of John Glasgow-3018, treating the latter provisionally as the father named with Agnes Martine in the 1693 Irvine child entry. The route adopts the existing comparison with John Glasgow-1434, indexed at Kilwinning on 6 July 1679 as child of John and Barbara Alason. Exact forename and surname, the neighbouring Ayrshire parishes, and a specific recorded child/parent pair make this a usable local model. It is not a merge or an identification of all events currently collected under either account. If the 1679 event was an infant baptism, that child would have been only fourteen by the 1693 entry. This is a serious weakness. Baptism of an older child would allow an older father, but no evidence establishes such a baptism; neither an earlier birth nor unusually young fatherhood is asserted as fact. The current circa-1675 birth is an inherited estimate, not independent support for the match.

John Glasgow-551, the John said in the later family history to have found a home in County Tyrone, is selected as a very uncertain working father of John Glasgow-3960, gentleman of Gortigillagh, County Leitrim, recorded in 1728. This develops the comparison already recorded in both case files. Keeping their current estimated generations separate gives about 1681 for the older John and about 1705 for the witness: a possible 24-year father–son interval. The proposed connection gives the Leitrim household a testable place alongside the early Irish family tradition. Its preference over an identity match depends on retaining those two estimated generations; neither birth year is independent evidence for paternity. The same uncommon surname and an early Irish setting support investigating kinship, but do not determine its degree. There is no named-father clause or documented Tyrone–Leitrim migration, and no place of birth is inferred from this link.

John Glasgow-1065 is selected as the uncertain working father of John Glasgow-2467, the John recorded with Mary Auld at Kilwinning for Andrew’s baptism on 26 October 1746 and James’s on 19 August 1750. The later John’s existing biography already suggests descent from John Glasgow-2463, an old parent reference with a 16 September 1683 Kilwinning date. The current captured family fields of the older household’s children point to John Glasgow-1065, whose profile carries that same 1683 date and the Jean Wyllie household. This resolves the intended candidate account; it is not a new historical father statement. A specific route is the recorded John Glasgow-2464, baptised at Kilwinning on 19 December 1703 to John Glasgow and Jean Wylie, residence Chappell. Treat that child provisionally as the later Mary Auld husband. If baptised in infancy, he would have been about 42 and 46 at the two known children’s baptisms, compatible ages for a father. The later profile’s before-1728 estimate permits this earlier birth. Exact name, parish, an already recorded descent suggestion and a documented child with named parents give a testable family model. No record yet establishes that the child and adult were the same man.

James Glasgow-3526 is selected as the uncertain working father of John Glasgow-2847, husband of Margaret Anderson and father of the West Calder children recorded from 1745 to 1755. The route provisionally identifies that adult with John Glasgow-3525, indexed at neighbouring Kirknewton and East Calder on 31 March 1717 with father James. The parish setting, exact forename and surname, and feasible generation favour this concrete local childhood over an unidentified origin: if baptised near birth in 1717, John would have been about 28 in 1745 and 38 in 1755. The later family also contains a James, although a common repeated forename does not independently establish a grandfather. No register entry yet joins the child to Margaret Anderson’s husband. This is a low-confidence identity-based parent model, not a proved father clause for the adult.

Patrick Glasgow-1440, represented by the Gordon Patrike baptism of 1667, is selected as a very uncertain working father of Patrick Glasgow-3920 of the Kilclone memorial. The memorial’s age 60 at death in May 1754 puts the younger Patrick’s birth around 1694. If the Gordon baptism was near birth, the older Patrick would have been about 27 then: an ordinary father–son interval. The matching Patrick/Patrike and Glasgow/Glasco name pair supplies a specific older candidate rather than an invented ancestor. This is a very weak generational model; neither name recurrence nor a feasible age establishes paternity. There is no reviewed deed, parish entry, probate clause, occupation or shared associate connecting Gordon or Stitchel to Kilclone. No migration or Scottish birthplace is newly established for the Meath man, and the catalogue is not a complete census of older Patricks.

James Glasgow-1025 is selected as the very uncertain working father of James Glasgow-2988, the 1766 Corvanaghan householder, through preferred provisional identity with James Glasgow-1024 of Moneymore. The existing Corvanaghan biography already retains the Moneymore man as a compatible candidate: the places are roughly nine miles apart, the name matches and their circa 1720/1722 births are estimates rather than a real two-year conflict. The 1766 Irish occurrence can precede the compiled 1770 immigration claim associated with the Moneymore family; no post 1766 Irish occurrence has been assigned to the Corvanaghan man. This is a weak locality and chronology preference, not proof of emigration or identity. The older James is already an uncertain father in the Moneymore pedigree. Extending that attachment gives the Corvanaghan account a conditional place in the same family, without inventing an intermediate generation. It inherits two major uncertainties: adult identity and the older pedigree itself.

Caleb Glasgow-363 is selected as the very uncertain working father of Lemuel Glasgow-2581. The case combines a local surname household, a compatible older generation and the same Currituck–Pasquotank setting. Lemuel’s November 1833 pension declaration says he was born in Currituck, moved to Pasquotank as an infant and remained there until moving to Randolph about 1803. William Glasgow-428’s previously reviewed 1746 Currituck will names a son Caleb. The two modern Caleb accounts, Glasgow-363 and Glasgow-830, both cite a Pasquotank will of 1803. These details make the established local Caleb family a useful preferred home for Lemuel over an otherwise unidentified father. They do not put Caleb in Lemuel’s infant household or name his parents. The preference for Glasgow-363 is generational: its circa 1726 birth allows a father aged about 27 in 1753; Glasgow-830’s circa 1740 birth would give about 13. Neither Caleb birth is established by a birth record here, and Lemuel himself said he had no age record and only believed he was born in 1753. The younger estimate therefore lowers the second account’s preference without excluding it. No baptism, guardianship, deed or pension statement names Caleb as Lemuel’s father. A collateral connection to Caleb, another local Glasgow father or an unrelated Glasgow immigrant remains possible. This is a low-confidence named-family hypothesis, not a documented father clause.

Glasgow-2868 is selected as the very uncertain working father of Glasgow-395. The preferred model identifies Moores-284’s husband with the Robert Glasgow who acted jointly with Joshua Hartshorn over a Cecil County plantation in 1786, then places him in the local Glasgow-2868–Hartshorne-320 family. The joint Glasgow/Hartshorn association gives a more specific family-network clue than surname and county alone. Robert’s estimated circa 1750 birth also fits James’s circa 1720 generation and the existing Cecil children’s mid-century dates. The Harford family context and Cecil land occurrence concern neighboring Maryland counties. This is a conditional reconstruction, not a father statement in either notice.

The existing father relationship from Glasgow-3012 to Glasgow-3610 is now documented locally for the record-defined 1649 child. The supplied Scotland’s People index, Kirknewton and East Calder OPR 690/10/14, FR 15, names JOHNE GLASGOW as parent of the child JOHNE indexed on 22 April 1649. The preserved FamilySearch VQ4K-X6G account agrees on the child, father, parish and date. These are two presentations of the same underlying register, not independent records. Glasgow-3610 is specifically the adult-father account defined by that entry. No inference from age or surname is needed for that parental role.

Robert Glasgow-1156 is now assessed as the probable father of James Glasgow-1150, the Edinburgh weaver. Grant’s 16 June 1641 apprenticeship names James’s father Robert and places the entry at Wester Duddingston with William Crichtoun and master William Sclaitter. The 20 June 1649 burgess admission repeats Sclaitter’s name and the exact apprenticeship date, securely connecting the recorded son to the adult weaver. The Robert buried at Duddingston on 17 January 1647 fits the father’s name, parish and preceding generation, six years after the apprenticeship and before James’s independent household began in 1649. Taken together, the specific local father and the Duddingston burial favour one Robert over an otherwise unattested second contemporary Robert in that parish. The previous assessment treated the lack of a unique identifier as a reason to stop at plausible; the combined argument warrants probable, while remaining an inference. The apprenticeship proves James’s father was Robert; identifying that father with the burial account Glasgow-1156 is probable rather than documented. The burial index gives no age, son, wife or occupation, and burial in the parish does not itself prove residence at Wester Duddingston. A second local Robert remains possible. The two craft entries are a linked identity chain, not two independent statements naming the father. The exact scope of “servitor” in the printed apprenticeship wording need not decide the inference: the entry supplies the father’s name and Duddingston association. No mother is identified, so Deborah Ivey is not upgraded. Robert’s unsupported Archibald-1097 ancestry and his compatible identification with Andrew-3163’s recorded son Robert-4006 remain separate questions. Neither the later Fisherrow sasine identity nor the Edinburgh weaver’s possible Lindsaylands continuation is needed for this father conclusion.

Hugh Glasgow-548 and Margaret McCullough-1964 are assessed as the probable parents of Hugh Glasgow-540, the emigrant whose Pennsylvania will was made in 1827 and proved in 1831. William Melanchthon Glasgow’s family history, p.2, explicitly names the elder Hugh and Margaret as the married parents of John, Robert and their youngest son Hugh, born in County Londonderry in 1739. Page 3 follows this younger Hugh’s household through John, whom the author calls his grandfather, and its emigration in 1796. This is specific descendant testimony about a named family, rather than a parent invented from dates or a shared surname. The younger Hugh’s recorded will independently names the same four sons John, Hugh, Alexander and Robert, and daughter Nancy, within the corresponding Pennsylvania household. That agreement supports the family history’s identification of the emigrant and the reliability of its nearer family relationships. It does not independently name his parents. The explicit family account, consistent household identity and feasible generations together warrant probable parentage rather than leaving the father and mother ungraded. Parentage rests on one retrospective family account; later online copies and family trees are derivatives, not independent witnesses. Its author gives no Irish baptism or marriage source, and its 1824 death claim is contradicted by Hugh’s signed 1827 will and 1831 probate. The 1733 marriage, 1739 birth, older Hugh’s circa-1706 birth and Margaret’s imported vital estimates retain their separate evidence limits. The two adult Hugh Glasgow householders in Tamlaght O’Crilly in 1740 support an earlier local surname generation, but the return supplies no kin or townland. Entry 1272 remains a leading compatible identity for the elder Hugh; collector order beside Ellis and McCullough names is not proof of adjoining homes or of Margaret’s father. No particular 1740 householder or the 1772 subscriber is selected as this man. The 1827 will does not name the testator’s parents or his wife; it therefore cannot independently establish Margaret’s maternity or Sally Blair’s identity. No John-551 parentage, older William/Covenanter ancestry, Cameron origin story, or connection to Adam of Inishrush is upgraded. The two brothers retain their existing links and grades: John-549’s captured confident flags are not counted as new upgrades, and Robert-550’s separate life remains unverified.

The existing Moneymore father account, Glasgow-1024, is assessed as the probable father of Robert Glasgow-12 and, by inference through their established brotherhood, Arthur Glasgow-649 and Joseph Glasgow-1543. The catalogue description of David Faris’s 1990 genealogy explicitly identifies the Adams County emigrant Robert (1749–1839) as a son of a James resident at Moneymore. It identifies a particular father and son, rather than offering a same-name local candidate. The family letter of 6 November 1806 printed by Faris names Arthur and Robert as Joseph’s brothers; Joseph’s 1831 will independently identifies Arthur as his deceased brother and the younger Robert as Arthur’s son. These sources distinguish the two Roberts and establish the sibling group to which the father attribution can reasonably extend. Robert’s pension supports the County Derry setting and 1769 migration. The approximate generations are compatible; the circa-1722 birth estimate is not independent evidence. The positive father attribution and established family group together warrant probable parentage, while remaining below documented or certain. The father attribution survives here through a catalogue abstract of a retrospective genealogy; the book’s underlying parentage notes and a contemporary Irish parent record have not been inspected. The letter and will corroborate the sibling group, not the father’s name independently. Glasgow-1024 is used for its record-defined Moneymore father role: the inherited dates, Mary Harkness marriage, 1770 immigration, 1804 naturalisation, older James pedigree and proposed Corvanaghan identity are separate questions. The Corvanaghan identity and older father remain very uncertain. No probability is assigned to those claims by this review. The same father is inferred across the three established paternal-surname siblings; no evidence for different fathers has been identified. Other proposed siblings, including James-3305, John and Mary, and the proposed Adam connection are not upgraded.

The existing Moneymore father account, Glasgow-1024, is assessed as the probable father of Robert Glasgow-12 and, by inference through their established brotherhood, Arthur Glasgow-649 and Joseph Glasgow-1543. The catalogue description of David Faris’s 1990 genealogy explicitly identifies the Adams County emigrant Robert (1749–1839) as a son of a James resident at Moneymore. It identifies a particular father and son, rather than offering a same-name local candidate. The family letter of 6 November 1806 printed by Faris names Arthur and Robert as Joseph’s brothers; Joseph’s 1831 will independently identifies Arthur as his deceased brother and the younger Robert as Arthur’s son. These sources distinguish the two Roberts and establish the sibling group to which the father attribution can reasonably extend. Robert’s pension supports the County Derry setting and 1769 migration. The approximate generations are compatible; the circa-1722 birth estimate is not independent evidence. The positive father attribution and established family group together warrant probable parentage, while remaining below documented or certain. The father attribution survives here through a catalogue abstract of a retrospective genealogy; the book’s underlying parentage notes and a contemporary Irish parent record have not been inspected. The letter and will corroborate the sibling group, not the father’s name independently. William’s 1746 Currituck will expressly names Caleb as his son and Abiah and Elizabeth as daughters. The existing Abiah and Elizabeth profiles share the named father, Currituck setting and compatible childhood generation; neither has a conflicting identity. Their father links are documented. The two Caleb profiles repeat the same FamilySearch identity and later Pasquotank will account, indicating possible duplicates. Both fit William’s named son sufficiently for probable father assessments, but they represent one historical son candidate, not two independently proved sons. The will survives here through a checked published transcription; the manuscript has not been newly inspected. Abiah’s competing 1730/1738 estimates and Elizabeth’s 1741 date are not proved by it. Caleb’s conflicting 1726/circa-1740 births, 1781/1804 deaths and Gregory/Sawyer spouse accounts remain unresolved. The 1803 Pasquotank will does not name Lemuel; his very uncertain selected link to Caleb-363 and alternative Caleb-830 retain that grade. Susanah is William’s named wife, but the will does not establish her as mother of every child; no mother is upgraded. Lowdenner is not equated with the named Sarah or unborn child. William’s own father remains unproved.

The family history explicitly calls John a son of William and introduces Hugh, the Tyrone-born weaver, among John’s sons. These are specific parent statements in a continuous pedigree, not parents supplied from a shared surname. The nearer part of that account identifies the Hugh–McCullough family and the younger Hugh’s Pennsylvania household, whose children agree with the independently inspected 1827 will. That household correlation supports the account’s family knowledge without independently proving the two earlier fathers. With the retained generations compatible and no conflicting parent account identified for these traditional roles, William–John and John–Hugh warrant probable local assessments. The preference is for the particular family-history accounts, not an identification with other same-name Scottish or Irish records. Both earlier father names come from one later family narrative; they are not two independent confirmations. John’s circa-1681 birth is calculated and William’s circa-1655/1656 date is estimated, so neither is corroboration. The 1740 return cannot distinguish the two Hugh householders or name their parents. No contemporary record identifies John-551 or William-591 in these roles. The narrative’s Cameron surname-origin and 1689 military story are unverified and are not used as parentage evidence. William’s selected uncertain Inveresk/Cavers identity and Robert-2462 father hypothesis remain separate. John-3960’s very uncertain placement and the alternative that the two Johns are one person remain unchanged. No mother, wife, new date, migration or exact 1740 identity is inferred.

The preferred local working parents of the Duddingston Robert are now Andrew Glasgow and Elizat Stevinsoun, through possible identity with their recorded son Robert-4006. The accepted 1597/8 testament expressly names Robert as Andrew’s son by Elizat and makes provision until he reached age. A minor then can fit the adult generation of the Robert buried at Duddingston in 1647 and the probable father of James the Edinburgh weaver. The retained circa-1582 and 1597/before-1597 dates are estimates or bounds, not two exact birth records in conflict. On the maintained, queried Calder-area reading of Andrew’s residence, this offers a positive named-child family candidate in the relevant broad Lothian comparison. The earlier Archibald/Isobell pair has no record naming the Duddingston Robert as its child. Prefer the recorded Corsoun family as the uncertain route, with both former parents retained as alternatives. The 1598 child and the Duddingston adult remain separate WikiTree profiles with an uncertain identity comparison; no merge is inferred. No holding, occupation, wife or named-relative bridge equates them, and the Corsoun/Calder place reading itself remains queried. A different local Robert, including the separate Ninian-son account Robert-1027, remains a comparison. Ninian’s son keeps his proved parents and is not conflated with Andrew’s named son. Elizat’s maternity is direct for the recorded child only; it is uncertain for the Duddingston adult because it depends on the same identity hypothesis. Archibald’s and Isobell’s biological parentage is not disproved. James-1150’s probable father assessment, all other selected families, and the adult’s existing vital fields remain unchanged. Two modern Robert accounts can represent one historical son; they are not independent evidence for two sons.
The accepted 1597/8 testament explicitly names Robert as Andrew’s son by Elizat his wife. This documents the record-defined family roles; no later adult identity or exact birth date is established.

Alexander’s 1673 Kirknewton birth/baptism index explicitly names father Alexander Glasgow. The existing Alexander-3118 account is the same-parish man indexed marrying Margaret Smith in 1667, six years earlier, with a compatible father generation and a later Agnes child association in 1677. The exact father name, parish and ordered household chronology together favour that existing adult as the named father. Assess the attachment as probable rather than leaving it ungraded. This is an inference identifying the indexed father with the 1667 adult; the child entry alone does not identify that adult by wife, trade or property. Another Alexander could have fathered the 1673 child. The marriage and baptism supply no inspected cross-reference, and the father’s circa-1650 birth is an estimate, not an age statement. Margaret Smith is not named as mother in the reviewed 1673 entry and receives no maternity upgrade. Andrew-1546 remains an uncertain proposed son of the older Alexander. Alexander-1141 remains an unproved child of the 1673 Alexander; the latter himself remains a possible older father behind the 1721–1732 child series. The 1673 birth/baptism dates, the 1701 and 1705 marriages and the later children’s maternity questions are retained. The older John-3610 father route is not strengthened.

The accepted Kilwinning parish transcripts name Robert Glasgow and Mary Simson as the parents of Hugh in 1716, George in 1719 and Jean in 1722. The existing 1715 Kilwinning marriage index names Robert Glasgow and Mary Simpson; ordinary Simson/Simpson spelling variation, the repeated parental pair and the ordered 1715–1722 family sequence identify one record-defined household. George and Jean also share Byrehill residence. These records document both parents for each indexed child, not merely a spouse inferred as mother. The three child profiles already represent those checked entries, so their father and mother assessments can be marked documented. These are previously accepted derivative register transcripts and indexes; no fresh original image reading or new record discovery is claimed. The three transcripts derive from one parish register and are not independent sources. Hugh’s transcript has no residence field; Byrehill is not newly assigned to him. The FMP page references and the separately retained ScotlandsPeople references remain literal provider locators. This household proof does not newly identify the adult Robert with the 1678 child, prove ancestry above either parent, or identify any child with a later adult. No date, birthplace, spouse, occupation, live parent field or saved certainty flag changes.

Prefer the Glasgow child baptised on 19 June 1614 and the Archibaldus Glasgua who graduated M.A. in 1635 as the earlier identity of the Donegal cleric. The uncommon full name, compatible age at graduation, clerical career and 1639 Irish clerk occurrence form a coherent Scottish-to-Irish career. A baptism in 1614 places him at about 21 in 1635 and 25 in 1639. These are conditional ages, not separately recorded ages. No incompatible parentage or simultaneous Scottish household is identified for this proposed cleric. The other known same-generation Scottish Archibald, the Leith man Glasgow-3078, has a separately traced craft career: apprentice to cordiner Thomas Park in October 1639 and shoemaker/heir in May 1647. That positive career sequence makes him a weaker fit to the 1635 graduate and Irish clerk than the 1614 Glasgow child. It is a ranking argument, not an absolute exclusion or an assertion that a man could never change occupation. The Irish testator is securely the Ramelton/Rathmalton cleric by exact name, residence and profession. Assess his existing George Glasgow and Margaret Steuart parent links as probable, reflecting the probable Scottish childhood identification. The baptism explicitly names both parents, so maternity has its own record basis rather than being inferred from George’s spouse field. No Irish record reviewed names Archibald’s Scottish parents or university. The graduation and 1639 clerk entry do not themselves state the 1614 baptism date. Another Archibald remains possible. This is a preferred combined identity, not documented migration or proof that every early Scottish and Irish occurrence is one man. The quoted baptism witnesses are reused from the maintained reading, not newly checked against an image. Margaret’s own Stewart ancestry, George’s wider family, and the 1647–1661 ministry chronology retain their existing grades.

Betham’s inspected abstract of the April 1673 will of Archibald Glasgow, clerk of Rathmalton, explicitly identifies Thomas Glasgow as his eldest son. Prefer the existing Thomas of Lifford/Raphoe account for that son: the exact uncommon name, the adjacent Donegal setting and the next adult generation fit the independently documented Raphoe-linked court case of 1684, Lifford occurrence of 1689 and Ballindrait/Shannon deeds of 1692–1695. The 1692 Creighton court association and later estate material strengthen the continuity of that adult Thomas account; they are not independent statements of his parentage. The full local and generational fit warrants a probable father link to Archibald. A further unique estate or household identifier would strengthen it, but its absence does not require leaving this coherent family at merely uncertain. Betham gives the son no age, residence, spouse or estate. He could be another Thomas, so the Lifford identification remains inferred rather than documented. The profile’s before-1671/circa-1670 birth estimates are not ages supplied by the abstract or court records and are not used as proof of either identity or exclusion. No maternity is assigned to Thomas from Elizabeth’s status as Archibald’s wife. Nathaniel and George remain Thomas’s separately assessed children; the later Killybegs James and Belfast Captain James are not made relatives by this review.

Select Thomas Glasgow-3556 of Lifford/Raphoe as the uncertain working father of James Glasgow-3001. Thomas is an established Donegal legal/property actor from the 1684 Raphoe-linked court occurrence through the 1692–1695 Shannon/Ballindrait deeds and the 1701 Exchequer continuation. James belongs to a later dated Donegal account under 1728. The same uncommon surname, regional continuity and compatible succession of legal/property and revenue roles make Thomas a useful preferred existing father account. This extends the recorded Ramelton–Lifford family into the otherwise unattached collector account without inventing an intermediary. It is a regional and generational inference: none of these records names James as Thomas’s son. The record dates are not measured ages. The 1728 entry may carry an earlier deceased or dismissed officer’s balance, so it cannot select a generation precisely. Archibald Glasgow-1101, Thomas’s probable father, remains a concrete older-family alternative: James might be Thomas’s younger brother or another kinsman rather than his son. An unrelated Donegal or wider Ulster Glasgow family remains possible. The Tyrone James Glasgow-1025 and Belfast Captain James Glasgow-3172 are not merged with this collector or excluded solely by their unproved birth estimates and parent fields. No Scottish-to-Irish migration, exact age, mother, spouse or child of James is inferred. Thomas’s existing probable Archibald father and his other children keep their separate assessments.

Prefer the named George of Mureistoun as James Glasgow-991’s probable father. George is recorded at Mureistoun in the 1586 Calder obligation; the accepted 1605 original-register reading places James’s household in probable Muirestoun and names an adult George Glasgow as witness to the baptism of James’s son George. The earlier review already assessed the two adult George occurrences as probably one man. The same uncommon surname, the probable same holding across nineteen years, and the older name-bearer’s personal participation in the younger household favour lineal family continuity. Father is the preferred degree: an older established man followed by James’s child-bearing household is a normal two-generation sequence, and the child’s George name is compatible with that reconstruction. This is a combined locality/household inference, not three independent proofs or a compulsory naming rule. The 1605 witness’s residence and age are unstated, and Muirestoun remains a probable reading/location. Shared holding names do not prove a legal title transfer. Father, uncle, older brother, cousin and neighbour remain genuine alternatives. The 1586 obligation does not establish muster attendance, and neither record states that George was James’s father. The George name and witness role are supporting context, not direct kinship. Andrew Glasgow-3163 remains an unselected uncertain father alternative; his 1597/8 testament names Robert, Marion, Jonet and Isobel, not James. The George comparison supplies a closer holding-and-witness association than the broader Andrew/Calder model, without proving that Andrew could not be James’s father.

For the working tree only, select William Glasgow-3522 as George of Mureistoun’s uncertain father through the surviving possible identification with the Glasgow merchant George Glasgow-1099. Protocol 2903 explicitly names that merchant’s deceased father William; protocol 2916 gives his mother and curator. The same rare full name and compatible 1586 generation make the merchant an existing-profile comparison for the Mureistoun man. The father proof belongs to the merchant: transferring it to the Mureistoun account depends entirely on the unproved identity. This is a testable named upstream route, not direct evidence of a Calder-to-Glasgow movement or a newly proved son of William. The merchant was a minor in 1586, with the accepted approximate birth range 1565–1572. If James’s conventional circa-1575 birth were established, that would conflict with his being the merchant’s son. James’s birth is unrecorded: a later birth in the 1580s can fit the 1605 fatherhood and, toward the earlier end of George’s range, ordinary fatherhood in the previous generation. Those are compatibility examples, not new birth estimates. The 1598 marriage-contract comparison does not prove a first marriage or identify James’s mother. No date is altered to make this route fit. George-1099 stays a compatible candidate; there is no merge, no second distinct George son claimed for William, and no automatic transfer of Margaret Herbesoun or a wife as mother. If the two Georges are different men, William’s upstream placement must be reconsidered. The retained George Glascoe-36 and George-3171 comparisons remain open on their actual source limits.

Prefer John Glasgow-3193 of the Corsankell/Kilwinning family as Hugh Glasgow-1603’s uncertain working father. This materializes the leading Ayrshire placement already argued in the maintained five-generation map. The 1571 Corsinkell deed expressly names John as James elder’s son; the earlier Kilwinning tenant appearances are attributed to him as probable. Hugh’s surviving profile account describes an Ayrshire progenitor, his son’s account is centred on Kilwinning, and the following households lie in Kilwinning, Ayr and Kilbirnie. These successive local settings favour the documented nearby family over the existing Mid Calder/Inveresk father attachment, which depends on an online tree and has no movement, household or property bridge. A John-to-Hugh-to-John sequence is compatible supporting context, not a naming rule. Father is selected as a revisable one-generation model, rather than leaving the previously preferred local route only in prose. Hugh remains a tree-derived generation: no inspected contemporary record securely identifies him, names his father or establishes his own c.1600 birth. John’s before-1540 boundary means a birth for Hugh near 1600 would make him an older father, around 60 or more; a grandson or collateral position may fit better. Neither date is changed to fit. An earlier Hugh birth is possible but is not adopted as a new estimate, and no missing person is invented. The 1571 John is documented as a son, while his additional Kilwinning identity is only probable. John’s brother James Glasgow-3921, another local Glasgow family, an omitted generation and the former James Glasgow-991 placement remain alternatives. This is stronger locality reasoning, not a probable or proved father assessment. The 1677 deed-index Hugh, preacher of the gospel, remains an unresolved identity comparison and supplies no evidence for this father choice.

Select James Glasgow-1970 of the Cookstown Mitchell family as John Glasgow-2539 of Gortin’s uncertain working father, through the existing possible identification with John Glasgow-1968. The 1879 Hillsdale history specifically identifies James and his Mitchell wife as parents of John, a farmer near Cookstown. The Gortin account supplies another John in the same Derryloran/Cookstown locality and an earlier compatible father generation. The maintained Hillsdale research already lists Gortin John as a possible duplicate. This is a positive named-son comparison in the relevant family and locality, stronger than an arbitrary father chosen only from the surname. Prefer this existing family as a revisable home for the 17-profile Gortin branch; retain both John accounts separately. The identity is uncertain. The Hillsdale histories describe John and Jane’s seven children as Robert, Mary A., William, John, Bessie, James and Margaret; the Gortin account instead links Francis, Hugh, Letitia and Samuel. No child has been matched across those sets. An earlier union could explain different couple-based lists, but none is established here and no additional marriage is invented. If the seven-child account was intended as an exhaustive lifetime list for John, the extra Gortin group would conflict with it. The Gortin before-1771 birth boundary comes from Samuel’s reported 1792 birth; the Hillsdale c.1778 father estimate is younger. Literal 1778 fatherhood of a 1792 child would be about 14 and is a serious constraint. These are reconstructed ages and estimates, not two original birth entries; both are retained, without silently shifting either date. Sarah MacNeece’s status as the Gortin man’s widow and Jane’s identity also require testing; no mother is transferred to Gortin John and no wife is added or replaced. Another local John, a collateral relationship, or different father remain alternatives. The 1700s and 1800s family accounts do not independently prove these two Johns identical.

Select the older James Glasgow-1025 account as the Cookstown progenitor James Glasgow-1970’s uncertain working father, conditional on the existing Corvanaghan/Moneymore family model. The c.1700 and c.1730 estimates allow a father–son generation. James-1970 is already a surviving possible identity for the Cookstown-area Corvanaghan James-2988, whose selected working father is James-1025 through the separate Moneymore comparison. Extending that same unproved pedigree gives the Mitchell account a consistent, revisable place in the broader family. The district context comes from those Cookstown/Corvanaghan/Moneymore comparisons, not from the 1759 index. This is an inherited family hypothesis with no independent father record for the Mitchell progenitor. No will, lease or baptism names the Cookstown James as the older James’s son. The reviewed PRONI detail says Drumcarn, County Tyrone, not Drumearn, and gives 17 January 1759 without age or kin; the modern profile identity and meaning of that date remain unresolved. It cannot corroborate Drumearn residence, a death date, or this father choice. The older and younger James accounts may themselves be duplicates rather than separate generations; if established, the father edge must collapse. The existing older pedigree and the Corvanaghan/Moneymore identity remain unproved. The 1879 history reports Scotland-to-Cookstown migration about 1750, while the older James’s profile is placed in Tyrone; neither a return journey nor that Scottish birthplace is established here. Multiple James and William householders appear in the 1740 Derryloran return, and two James men appear at Drumearn in 1766. William or another local father, a collateral link and a separate Scottish origin remain alternatives. Mary Harkness is not transferred to the Mitchell account, and Margaret Rutherford is not assigned as its mother. James-1970, James-2988, James-1024 and the older James-1025 remain separate possible overlapping reconstructions, not independently proved sons or households.

Assess the Hillsdale record-defined core as probable: James Glasgow-1970 as John Glasgow-1968’s father, Unknown Mitchell as that John’s mother, and James and Mitchell as spouses. The 1879 account explicitly gives those relationships; the 1888 sketches identify the same John–Jane household through sons William and John, their seven-child group and Michigan history. These are detailed late family accounts, not contemporary Scottish or Irish birth/marriage entries. Conflicting Scottish versus Tyrone origins, c.1778 dating and 1844/1848 immigration years limit the life-history reconstruction. estimates.basis: Select James Glasgow (Glasgow-1238), the father recorded with Elizabath/Elizabeth Tait at Stichill, as Robert Glasgow’s possible working father, at 34%. The couple’s maintained marriage citation is dated 25 January 1740; their David and James children are indexed in June 1744 and July 1746. Robert’s estimated 1745 birth fits that family generation and could fall between those events; it is not a dated baptism. Stichill and Eccles/Leitholm belong to the same small Borders district, and the later Swinton entry attributed to the James/Tait couple offers a further local comparison. Robert’s earlier son James supplies a modest naming clue consistent with this father; a common forename cannot establish paternity. The combination favours this existing, record-defined family over the catalogue’s distant Kirknewton candidates, whose apparent proximity came from mapping Leitholm to South Leith. No inspected record names Robert as James’s son. This is a preferred, revisable hypothesis, with 34% subjective confidence, not a measured probability or a confident connection. Robert’s 1745 birth and 8 August 1800 death each have zero attached sources on the inspected FamilySearch tree. Neither date establishes an age or place of birth. The local 1745 estimate is retained unchanged. FamilySearch attaches John Glasgow (1720–1785, GFNP-FS8) and Agnes Spark (1722–deceased, K8CD-HCW) as parents; retain that alternative without treating a contributed tree as documentary proof. The evidential basis of that parent attachment has not yet been reviewed. Do not equate that John with the much older John Glasgow-1057, husband of Agnes Spark-330, from the matching names alone. James’s brother John Glasgow-1444, christened at Stichill in 1708, is another compatible local father-generation alternative with no presently inspected Robert link. An unrecorded local father or another kinship degree remains possible. The Swinton/1740 couple continuity and Robert’s own early life need testing. Elizabeth Tait is not selected as Robert’s mother: her marriage and maternity of other children do not identify his mother. Robert is not merged with an earlier child, and James’s existing older ancestry retains its own uncertainty.

Select John Glasco of Drumearn (Glasgow-2990) as Robert Glasgow-1189’s possible working father, at 31% subjective confidence. The specific reported father name John favours a John comparison over the automated leading candidate James Glasgow-1970. The actual 1766 Derryloran return places John at Drumearn beside two James Glasco households, three years before Robert’s estimated birth. That supplies a real Tyrone father-generation account compatible with the reported origin. John’s circa-1750 local estimate and the contributed father’s 1745 year are both unproved; either permits fatherhood around 1769, and no date is changed to fit. The estimate assesses the whole proposition that the documented householder was the reported father. It is not a rating of the census record, a statistical probability, or a product of the uncertain ancestry above John. There are two unresolved steps: whether the contributed John/Margaret parentage is correct, and whether that John was the Drumearn householder. A common given name, estimated generation and claimed county cannot establish identity. The 1766 return supplies no wife, child, age or parent; the nearby James entries do not identify John’s father. Robert’s Tyrone birthplace is not independently established by the inspected Geneanet page. John’s existing uncertain James Glasgow-2988 father is preserved, with no new support. The Cookstown reward subscriber of 1796 is an unresolved namesake comparison, with Robert Glasgow-3941 the stronger maintained candidate; that notice supplies no parent and is not used as proof that the Martinsburg man lived at Cookstown. The single Geneanet/Ancestry family-tree chain and its repetition in WikiTree are not independent witnesses. Retain another unidentified Irish John as a serious alternative. John Glasgow-3314, associated with Margaret Mill and the West Calder children of 1762–1770, matches both reported parental given names and a viable generation, but has no inspected Robert or Irish-origin bridge. His Scottish baptism and actual West Calder household are distinct facts; an unproved Irish birthplace is not a categorical exclusion. John Glasgow-4179 of Larne also fits the estimated generation; his known Rose Allan marriage does not prove there was no earlier Margaret, but no record connects him with Robert or Drumearn. James Glasgow-1970 has a Cookstown family tradition and a rare Julia/Julia Ann descendant-name resemblance; those are useful regional clues, but do not outweigh the specific reported John father name. The particular Alexander household is established at Kirknewton by the 1667 Margaret Smith marriage and the father-named Alexander and Agnes entries in 1673 and 1677. Andrew’s 1700 Christian Cook marriage and fatherhood of James in 1702 place his own adult household in the same parish, one generation later. The sustained parish setting and feasible household succession together favour this existing family. Andrew, Alexander and Agnes recur in the descendant branches, providing modest supporting context rather than an independent naming rule. This weighs a specific family against alternatives, rather than inferring fatherhood from surname and estimated ages alone. The 1685 birth is an unsourced estimate. Taken literally it makes Andrew about fifteen at the indexed 1700 marriage and seventeen at the 1702 christening. Those ages are possible, but they cannot independently support the pedigree. A birth earlier in the 1670s or early 1680s would also fit the adult events and Alexander’s family chronology; no replacement birth year is adopted. Alexander’s own circa-1650 birth is likewise an estimate. The argument rests chiefly on the recorded adult households, not on moving either birth date to fit.

estimates.basis: Select John Glasgow-2475 of the Irvine Isabell Kyle/Kelle household as the possible working father of James Glasgow-4157, Helen Nasmith’s partner, at 58% subjective confidence. estimates.scope: The 58% assesses the complete father proposition, including the uncertain baptism-to-adult identity. James Glasgow-4157’s before-1722 birth is an inherited adult-age estimate, not a 1722 birth or a hard biological boundary. Do not use that estimate to prefer or exclude a candidate. estimates.scope: The 96% concerns the record-defined father of the 1652 child and his identification with the adult father of the 1649 child. It does not identify that adult with the John baptised at Mid Calder in 1616, prove his own father, or establish Annah’s later identity as the 1676 bride. The transcripts name no mother. These are overlapping profile-identity propositions, not mutually exclusive biological fathers; the percentages must not be added or treated as independent evidence. Retain that account as an alternative and resolve the possible duplicate before any live family change. No profiles are merged.

Select William Glasgow-3586, the weaver at Achenyeards named as Jean’s father in the 1 October 1732 Dundonald baptism, as William Glasgow-4101’s possible father at 52% subjective confidence. The specific existing local household offers a more useful working placement than leaving the 1733 child isolated: the children share the uncommon surname and parish, their entries occur on nearby pages of the same register, and the boy’s William name agrees with the proposed father. The existing father account is already paired with Barbara Stevenson, the boy’s named mother, but that tree pairing has not been traced to an independent marriage or full-parent entry and is not counted as additional proof. The whole father proposition remains an indirect household reconstruction.
estimates.limitations: The 1733 transcript has no father field or residence; absence from a transcript does not establish what the manuscript contains or prove illegitimacy. The 1732 transcript names William, weaver at Achenyeards, but no mother. Do not manufacture birth dates to resolve it. Another Glasgow father, a different Barbara Stevenson, and two separate local families remain alternatives. Barbara’s identification with her own 1733 citation is strong; the adult couple and cross-child father assignment are separate inferences. No mother is assigned to Jean, no full-sibling claim is made, and the existing ungraded Jean-to-William father relationship is unchanged. The earlier Ayrshire William accounts Glasgow-1055, Glasgow-3288 and Glasgow-1061 remain compatible wider comparisons; estimated ages or missing family details do not exclude them. No record links this father to any of their birth families, so no upstream father is selected. No later newspaper, maritime or American identity is inferred for the child. Exact percentages are individual judgments, not measured frequencies. Original register images were not newly inspected and no live WikiTree edit is made.

estimates.basis: Select Thomas Glasco-144 as the Trinity student John’s probable working father at 63% subjective confidence. Select Isobell/Elizabeth Duffe (Duffe-18) as James Glasgow-4114’s probable working mother at 72% subjective confidence, through the preferred Edinburgh Duffe household. The 1696 apothecary apprentice and the 1699 youngest-son apprentice Thomas share the specific father description James Glasgow, weaver and burgess. Thomas’s maintained identification with the 1684 child of James and Isobell Duffe fits entry at almost fifteen. The supplied Edinburgh index gives a James to James Glasgow and Elizabeth Duffe on 16 March 1679, and another to James Glasgow and Issobell Duff on 18 April 1680. Either child fits the 1696 apprentice at seventeen or sixteen. Both childhood candidates therefore lead into a Duffe maternal household without requiring us to choose or merge the children. No mother is named in either apprenticeship, and neither James baptism is securely identified with the apprentice. The two maternal forenames may represent different women; Duffe-18 is retained as the existing qualified Isobell/Elizabeth household account, not proof that those names denote one woman. The later James may be the survivor, but no infant burial proves that. Another matching craftsman’s family, a half-brother relationship, another Duffe woman, and the unresolved cancelled 1690 Lindsayland apprenticeship remain alternatives. The 72% rates this whole maternal identification and stays below the father’s 82%; the father, brother and mother assessments share evidence and must not be multiplied as independent support.

estimates.basis: James Glasgow-2682, father of the Edinburgh Duffe household, probably represents the same adult as James Glasgow-1150, the weaver apprenticed on 16 June 1641 and admitted burgess on 20 June 1649: 70% subjective identity confidence. The 1696 James and 1699 youngest-son Thomas apprenticeships name a father James Glasgow, weaver and burgess of Edinburgh. Thomas’s maintained 1684 baptismal identification and the Duffe household’s James children of 1679 and 1680 fit those apprenticeship ages and the youngest-son order. The older craftsman independently has that specific craft and civic status, with an exact master/date cross-reference between his 1641 apprenticeship and 1649 admission. The maintained admission review found one matching admission, although this does not establish uniqueness. His marriages to Bessie Whyte on 6 July 1649 and Agnes Duncan on 11 November 1653, followed by Agnes’s burial as the weaver’s wife on 21 January 1674, permit a later Duffe household beginning in 1677. Successive marriages explain the wife sequence without requiring another same-name weaver and burgess. Select Robert Glasgow-1156 as James-2682’s probable working father at 61%, conditional on that preferred adult identity and the existing 86% identification of the 1641 apprentice’s named father Robert with the Duddingston account buried in 1647. This replaces only the former local Johnne Glasgow-1151 hypothesis, retained unselected at 26%. The live father was blank in the public check on 21 October 2026: the outstanding WikiTree action is a new probable father addition, not replacement of a live father. The 61% and 70% are subjective assessments of nested propositions, not independent confirmations or statistically calculated probabilities.
estimates.scope: The main weaknesses are a very long working life and late fatherhood through 1691, together with the absence of a marriage, prior-wife clause, address, witness or admission-date reference directly joining the Duffe husband to the 1649 burgess. The 1693 same-name weaver master is an inferred identification, not an independently dated identity bridge. Another younger Edinburgh weaver and burgess remains possible. The cancelled 1690 Lindsayland apprenticeship could concern the 1696 son, but its deceased father would conflict with assigning that father to the living 1693 master; resolve this before a merge. Retain both James profiles as accounts of potentially one adult, not two proved sons of Robert. Johnne-1151 remains an unselected younger-family alternative at 26%, alongside the James-3076/James-3077 and Annapill Glessie childhood route, John-1084’s Gordon family, and an unrecorded father. Those alternatives are conditional on the Duffe husband being a distinct younger man, not equally compatible with the preferred pre-1641 adult.
